newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Nikon sees recovery in stepper business.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Nikon sees recovery in stepper business.

text.p: Japan's Nikon Corp says it expects demand for its mainstay steppers -- machines for making memory chips -- to recover by late 1998.

"I think the business will remain tough in the first half of next fiscal year. But by the 1998/1999 business year, we should see a considerable recovery in demand for steppers," company president Shigeo Ono told Reuters in a recent interview.
Demand for steppers began to decline in mid-1996 due to a plunge in prices of 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips.
Nikon, which made its name in cameras, is the industry leader in stepper manufacturing in Japan. Steppers account for about 60 percent of its total sales.
The company is now banking on new excimer steppers for making next-generation 256 megabit and one gigabit DRAM chips.

Steppers print electric circuits on silicon wafers to make chips, and the excimer models can print lines as fine as 0.25 micron wide, compared with 0.35 micron for older models. A micron is one-millionth of a metre.
Ono said the company already has a backlog of orders for excimer steppers greater than its planned sales for the 1997/98 business year, starting on April 1.
He said it expects to ship about 200 excimer steppers in 1997/98, up from 40 to 50 in the current year.

Total shipments of steppers, including excimer models and the older steppers used for 16 megabit DRAM chips, in the year to March 31 will likely be about the same as the previous year, Ono said. Nikon shipped 565 units in 1995/96.
Ono said he hopes to further shift research and development resources from cameras to steppers, as Nikon expects its chip-equipment business to grow more than its camera business.

But he predicted that the camera division would turn profitable in the 1997/98 business year after losing money for three consecutive years. The improvement would be achieved by restructuring and a significant decline in the cost of developing and marketing new products.
"Our camera division will be in the black next business year, albeit by a small margin," said Ono.
Nikon has been moving staff from its camera division to the stepper business in recent years as part of restructuring.
Efforts to shift production overseas have also helped to make the camera division profitable again, Ono said.
Nikon currently makes about 30 percent of its cameras overseas. It aims to raise the ratio to 75 percent by the end of the 1998/99 business year.
It is considering setting up a joint venture in China with a local state-run firm in the next business year to make and sell cameras, Ono said. He did not elaborate.
Sales of cameras are expected to rise more than 20 percent in the year to March 31 and further grow by at least 10 percent in the next business year, Ono said.
As for company-wide earnings, Nikon expects to post sales of 295 billion yen and a parent current profit of 17 billion yen in the year to March 31.
Ono said the company's consolidated profit will likely be twice as big as parent profit and group-based return on equity would reach 12 percent in the current business year.
